query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HTXRD) is an effective method to evaluate high‐temperature oxidation behavior and phase stability in high‐entropy alloys because it enables real‐time monitoring of phase transformations and oxide scale formation as the temperature increases.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi or AlCoCrFeNi) with a known single-phase or multiphase structure obtained by standard processing (such as casting or homogenization).
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to an oxidizing environment while heating continuously and record diffraction patterns in real time.
generation.conditions: Heating from room temperature up to 1100 °C in either air or a controlled oxygen atmosphere with predetermined heating rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation or transformation of oxide phases (for example, the development of nonprotective manganese oxides or the emergence of protective spinel phases) together with any underlying phase changes of the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: HTXRD detects changes in diffraction peaks that indicate the onset of oxidation (via new oxide peaks) and phase transformation (via shifts or appearance/disappearance of matrix phase peaks). This correlates changes in the microstructure with oxidation kinetics and phase stability at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Distinct evolution in the XRD pattern will be observed—initially a stable pattern at room temperature, followed by the appearance of new peaks associated with oxide phases and changes in the matrix phase as temperature increases. This will allow quantification of oxidation rates and the identification of phase transformation temperatures.
generation.baseline: The initial XRD pattern of the pristine alloy measured at room temperature before exposure to high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The method may have limitations in detecting very low volume fractions of new phases or in systems where oxidation occurs too rapidly relative to the time resolution of the measurement.
generation.uncertainty: Sensitivity to minor phase changes and detection limits for ultra-thin oxide scales may require supplementation with other techniques (e.g., TGA or TEM) to fully confirm the oxidation mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a high-entropy alloy sample (with a well-characterized baseline phase structure) and subject it to a controlled high-temperature oxidizing environment while recording in situ XRD data. Simultaneously, perform complementary TGA and post-mortem microscopic analyses (e.g., SEM/EDS) to verify oxide formation.
measurements: Time- and temperature-resolved XRD patterns (tracking peak shifts, emergence of new peaks, or intensity changes)
Mass change via TGA to quantify oxidation kinetics
Microstructural characterization (SEM/EDS) of the oxidized surface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HTXRD does not show the expected emergence or evolution of oxide and matrix phase peaks—despite independent TGA and microscopic evidence confirming oxidation and phase transformation—then HTXRD would be considered insufficient to capture the high-temperature oxidation behavior and phase stability in the alloy.

Question: What are the time–temperature-dependent oxidation mechanisms and phase transformations of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy in vacuum and air environments, and how do they compare with thermodynamic predictions?. System: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (20 at.% each of Cr, Co, Fe, Mn, Ni). Processing: Arc melting and drop casting of 3 N purity elements in a vacuum of ~7 × 10⁻⁴ Pa followed by argon refilling to ~8.4 × 10⁴ Pa; annealing at 900 °C for 48 h; cold rolling to 1.6 mm thickness; mechanical and mirror polishing with 1 μm diamond suspension for in situ analysis. Test conditions: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) from 25 °C to 1100 °C at 15 °C/min heating rate with 5 min stabilization at 50 °C intervals; two environments: vacuum (~4.2 × 10⁻⁶ atm) and air (1.0 atm); CuKα radiation (λ = 0.154 nm), 40 kV, 40 mA, 2θ range 30–80°.
